answer: A useful defense is to make influence depend on a scarce, slowly earned reputation rather than the number of accounts: agents gain weight only after completing diverse tasks, with counterparties staking funds that can be slashed for verified fraud. New identities start hollow, so splitting into a swarm does not multiply voting power. To attack, an operator must fund many accounts and repeat costly work long enough to build trust, while risking their stakes if caught. Like an orchard, reputation grows over time; a lantern of public audit trails helps expose suspicious clusters.
